source.title: D2.4 Catalogue of measures for urban aquatic ecosystems rehabilitation
source.pages: Printed page numbers of the PDF (the number in the page header).
source.note: Matched by the StreamProof team from the Catalogue's own text; wording is paraphrased. The final choice of measure belongs to the OneAquaHealth DSS and the municipality. The Catalogue is about rehabilitating urban streams, not emergency response, so first-response checks are listed separately and are not from it.

4.2.1.title: In-stream self-purification enhancement
4.2.1.group: Essential chemical and water quality measures
4.2.1.what: Restore physical complexity in the channel (boulder clusters, riffle-pool sequences, macrophytes) so the stream aerates and cleans itself again.
4.2.1.limits: Needs a minimum baseflow, is weak in intermittent streams, and underperforms if nutrient inputs stay high. Must be paired with source control.

4.2.2.title: Sewer system and point-source improvements
4.2.2.group: Essential chemical and water quality measures
4.2.2.what: Find and fix what feeds pollution in: overflows, leaking or misconnected pipes, untreated discharges.
4.2.2.limits: High cost, long timelines, coordination between utilities and the municipality, and illicit connections that stay hidden.

4.2.3.title: Litter, plastic, and hydrocarbon control
4.2.3.group: Essential chemical and water quality measures
4.2.3.what: Traps and oil-water separators before outfalls, regular clean-ups, an emergency response for spills (absorbent barriers, containment), and behaviour measures such as signage and clean-up events.
4.2.3.limits: Needs regular maintenance, public behaviour and enforcement; separators need proper disposal of oily residue. The Catalogue notes that documented hydrocarbon-interception cases are scarce.

4.3.1.title: Removing barriers
4.3.1.what: Remove obsolete weirs, dams or culverts so water, sediment and species move freely again. The Catalogue notes that low-head barriers can hold stagnant water in dry spells, which favours mosquito breeding.
4.3.1.limits: Releases sediment downstream, can spread invasive species, leaves less water where a reservoir sat, and meets heritage or public attachment to the barrier.
4.3.1.evidence: stagnant water, providing favourable conditions for mosquito breeding

4.3.5.title: Constructed riffles
4.3.5.what: Size-sorted stones and boulders placed in the channel to restore a natural, flowing bed. The Catalogue lists mosquito reduction among its advantages.
4.3.5.limits: Floods can scour them, they need the right slope and discharge, and their benefits can be short-lived.

4.4.2.title: Citizen Science and educational partnerships
4.4.2.what: Involve residents, schools and associations in monitoring the stream, building stewardship and giving the municipality more data.
4.4.2.limits: Data quality varies and often needs expert validation; participation needs coordination and institutional backing.

4.4.4.title: Regulatory and behavioural measures for pollution reduction
4.4.4.what: Work with households, schools and businesses on proper disposal of oils, litter and chemicals, backed by municipal and utility governance.
4.4.4.limits: Change is slow and uneven, and needs enforcement and long-term political commitment.

4.7.1.title: Natural wastewater treatment plants
4.7.1.what: Constructed wetlands and soil filters that remove nutrients and limit algal growth by reducing light. An optional measure that prevents contamination; it is not part of rehabilitating the stream itself.
4.7.1.limits: Needs a large area, can clog, and can give off odour.

4.6.1.title: Rain gardens
4.6.1.caution: If poorly drained they can hold stagnant water that supports mosquito larvae. The Catalogue asks for well-draining substrate, no standing water for more than 48 hours, and regular maintenance.

4.6.2.title: Rainwater harvesting systems
4.6.2.caution: Tanks and gutters that are not maintained can breed mosquito larvae, more so in warm climates.

4.6.6.title: Vegetated swales
4.6.6.caution: Poorly designed or unmaintained swales may hold stagnant water, causing mosquito breeding or odour.

4.6.7.title: Retention ponds and floodable parks
4.6.7.caution: Poorly designed or unmaintained ponds may hold stagnant water, causing mosquito breeding or odour. The Catalogue also advises against ponds where none would exist naturally, to avoid attracting disease vectors.

first_response: Walk the reach to see whether a weir, culvert or blockage is holding the water back.
Photograph the pond edge and note how long the water has stood.

notes.text: The Catalogue recommends adding medically relevant Diptera to urban monitoring, alongside the usual biological indicators (section 2.3).

first_response: Ask the municipal vector-control team to inspect the ponded sections.
A larval dip survey at the ponded sections would confirm breeding.
Put up a temporary 'avoid contact' notice for people and dogs until it is checked.
Sample for cyanobacteria and toxins at an accredited laboratory.
Walk upstream to look for a discharge point or a spill.
Trace the source at storm-drain outfalls.
Notify the environmental authority; contain a spill quickly if one is under way.

notes.text: The Catalogue states that sewage should always go to a waste-water treatment plant and never directly to a stream or river.
notes.evidence: sewage waters should always be directed

odour.inferred: The Catalogue has no measure for odour itself. Sewage leaks and misconnections are its nearest entry, so this is the team's inference.
first_response: Walk the reach to locate the source.
Schedule a clean-up with local groups.

foam.inferred: The Catalogue has no measure for foam itself. Persistent foam can point to a pollution source, so the point-source entry is the nearest match; this is the team's inference.
first_response: Note whether the foam persists after 24 hours; sample if it does.

about.text: Citizen-science data quality "often needs expert validation" (Catalogue section 4.4.2). StreamProof is that validation layer: only expert-verified records feed a decision.
